# Northwind Co. — Payment Verification Policy

> Fictional example policy for the Training Content Studio golden example. Northwind Co. is not a real company.

- Document owner: Finance Controls & IT Security
- Policy number: FIN-SEC-07
- Version: 2.1
- Effective date: 2026-03-01
- Applies to: all Northwind Co. employees, contractors and temporary staff

## 1. Purpose

Business email compromise (BEC) and CEO fraud trick employees into sending money or changing bank details
by impersonating executives, colleagues or suppliers. This policy sets the checks every employee must make
before acting on a payment request or a bank-detail change.

## 2. Scope

This policy covers every request to make a payment, release a payment, buy gift cards or vouchers, or change a
supplier's, customer's or employee's bank details, whether the request arrives by email, chat, text message,
phone call or video call.

## 3. Verify by calling back a known number

3.1 Before you act on any request to make a payment or change bank details, call the requester back on a phone number that is already
on file in the Northwind supplier master or the company directory.

3.2 Never use a phone number, link or contact detail given in the request itself.

3.3 A request from an executive is verified the same way: call the executive back on their directory number or
confirm in person. Seniority is never a reason to skip verification.

3.4 If you cannot verify the request, do not make the payment or the change.

## 4. Two-person approval

4.1 Every payment of USD 10,000 or more needs approval from two authorised people before it is released.

4.2 Every change to bank details needs a second person to approve it after the callback, whatever the amount.

4.3 No one may split a payment into smaller amounts to stay below the USD 10,000 threshold.

## 5. Warning signs

Treat a payment request as suspicious if it shows any of these signs:

- urgency or pressure to pay today;
- a request to keep the payment secret or to bypass the normal process;
- new or changed bank details;
- an unusual payment method, such as gift cards;
- a sender address or reply-to address that does not match the usual one.

## 6. Report it

6.1 Report every suspicious payment request to IT Security straight away, using the Report Phishing button in Outlook
or by calling the IT Security hotline on extension 4400.

6.2 Do not reply to, forward or delete the suspicious message before reporting it.

6.3 If you think money has already been sent, report it to IT Security and Finance immediately. Fast reporting gives
the bank the best chance to stop the transfer.

6.4 No one will be blamed for reporting a request that turns out to be genuine.
